div.head: IV Atr 1
div.ab: Ealdredesgate et Cripelesgate (id est portas illas) obseruabant custodes.
Ealdredesgate et Cripelesgate (id est portas illas) observabant custodes.
Aldersgate und Cripplegate (d. h. jene Thore) hüteten als Wachen [die Londoner].
Aldersgate and Cripplegate (that is, those gates) were guarded as watchmen [by the Londoners].
The gates called Aldersgate and Cripplegate (i.e. the actual gates) were in the charge of guards.

note.seg: so T; Aaldretes. R; Aldretes MHk
so T; Aaldretes. R; Aldretes MHk

Die drei Tore Londons (ebd. 61) kommen hier zuerst vor; vgl. über eine Karte um 1250 aus St. Albans H. Hall Court life under Henry II. 27. 206.—Aldersgate street nördlich von St. Paul's, führt nw. aus der City hinaus; das Tor lag sw. von Cripplegate

The three gates of London (ibid. 61) appear here for the first time; cf., on a map of c. 1250 from St Albans, H. Hall Court life under Henry II. 27. 206.—Aldersgate Street, north of St Paul's, leads north-west out of the City; the gate lay south-west of Cripplegate

Cripplegate kommt in Urkk. a. 1068. c. 1080 vor bei Davis Reg. Agnorm. n. 22. XXVII.—Agsächs. heisst crypel ‘Krüppel’; Toller Suppl. [mit dem gleichlautenden Worte, das ‘enger Graben, Abzugsgrube’ bedeutet, verbindet man den Namen nicht]. Porta contractorum sagt Stow dafür. Nach Pauli (Bilder aus Alt-England 370) riefen dort Krüppel die Reliquien des h. Eadmund an. Ein anderes Crypelgeat liegt südlich bei Marlborough; * Urk. a. 934 Bi 699; vgl. Lethaby London bef. Conquest 187

Cripplegate occurs in charters a. 1068. c. 1080 in Davis Reg. Agnorm. n. 22. XXVII.—In Anglo-Saxon crypel means ‘cripple’; Toller Suppl. [the name is not connected with the homonymous word meaning ‘narrow ditch, drainage pit’]. Stow says Porta contractorum for it. According to Pauli (Bilder aus Alt-England 370) cripples there invoked the relics of St Eadmund. Another Crypelgeat lies just south of Marlborough; * charter a. 934 Bi 699; cf. Lethaby London bef. Conquest 187

Die anderen Citytore gab Heinrich IV. London zu bewachen; Norton Comment. on London 371; Birch Histor. char. of London 162. Bishopsgate ward von den Dänen, dann im 13. Jh. von Hanseaten bewacht; Höhlbaum Hans. Urkb. I 747. Vgl. über Stadttorwache allgemein Maitland Domesday 187; Gl Stadt 3a. 4

Henry IV gave the other City gates to London to guard; Norton Comment. on London 371; Birch Histor. char. of London 162. Bishopsgate was guarded by the Danes, then in the 13th cent. by the Hanseatics; Höhlbaum Hans. Urkb. I 747. Cf., on the guarding of town gates in general, Maitland Domesday 187; Gl Stadt 3a. 4

This is the earliest mention of these names in any extant document (see Lethaby, London before the Conquest, p. 86). Stow (Survey of London, ed. Kingsford, 1908, i. p. 33) records that he had read that in 1010 the body of King Edmund was brought into London at Cripplegate, ‘so-called of Criples begging there,’ but in the Memorials of St Edmund’s Abbey (Rolls Series, i. 43) it is said to have been brought a via quae Anglice dicitur Ealsegate. Cripplegate appears also in documents of 1068 and about 1080 (see Davis, Reg. Agnorm. Nos. 22, xxvii).
